title: Lightning Talk

speakers.name: Greg McCord
speakers.affiliation: Chief Security Officer, Confide Group (description: Cybersecurity Strategist and CISO Advisor, Confide Group)

thesis: CISOs under pressure from fast AI adoption feel overwhelmed, and a deliberate pause and different perspective is a better coping mechanism than spiraling or working 16-hour days chasing shiny objects.
summary: McCord uses his lightning slot to talk about mental health rather than technology. He recounts the start of the agentic rush at his previous employer, a technology company where he was CISO: leadership wanted to turn everything on, he argued for guardrails, and being against the grain left him isolated, followed by a management change that put him on the chopping block. He describes spiraling through self-doubt before concluding he was right because of customer data and other risks, then deciding to study the organization's culture and define his approach. He told his team to research every model in front of them quickly so they would not end up where he did. He then describes how he copes with feeling overwhelmed: step away from the keyboard, touch a surface with rough edges, and change his state of mind, drawing on somatic processing techniques from his therapist wife. He says he knows to stop when he is spending 16 hours a day chasing shiny objects and to return with more energy and a different angle. At Confide, building AI products and helping other CISOs roll out AI at scale, he says he can now share the process. He closes with a short audience breathing exercise, says he is nervous, and notes there are better and worse coping mechanisms.
argument: A CISO who pushes for guardrails during an AI rollout can end up isolated and professionally at risk, which produces an overwhelming spiral.
The feeling is normal and manageable: step away, change state, and come back to the problem with energy and a different perspective.
The experience pushed him to learn everything about AI and tell his team to do the same so they are not caught unprepared.
Having done this, he can now give other CISOs a process for rolling AI out at scale.

claims.claim: Pushing for guardrails when leadership wanted everything turned on put him against the grain of his organization, and a management change then left him on the chopping block.
claims.evidence: Personal account of his time as CISO at an unnamed technology company; no details of outcome beyond the spiral.

claims.claim: Stepping away from the keyboard, using a tactile reset and somatic processing techniques reduces the feeling of being overwhelmed and restores energy.
claims.evidence: His own practice and advice from his therapist wife; a short audience breathing exercise was offered as a demonstration.

claims.claim: Spending 16 hours a day chasing shiny objects while researching a problem is the signal that a break is needed.
He has a repeatable process for rolling out AI at scale that he is using at Confide with customers and will share with other CISOs.
claims.evidence: Stated but not described in the talk.

numbers.meaning: time he spends researching when chasing shiny objects, which he treats as the cue to stop

demos: A guided breathing exercise with the audience: eyes closed, a deep breath in, hold, release, then asking who felt a change in demeanor.

quotes.text: There's better coping mechanisms and there's not so great coping mechanisms.
quotes.speaker: Greg McCord

defense: Put guardrails in place before turning on AI features, especially where customer data is at stake.
Have the security team research every model they face early so the team is not caught unprepared.
Recognize overload and step away: leave the keyboard, change state, and return with a different perspective.
takeaways: On one operator's account, treat CISO overload during an AI rollout as an operational risk and give yourself and your team permission to pause.
On one operator's account, have the team learn the models in front of them early so that they can argue guardrails with knowledge rather than from the sidelines.
As one person's rule of thumb, use a concrete signal, such as 16-hour research days, to trigger a break.
limits: Speaker said he could talk about this for hours and limited the talk to a short personal account; no process for AI rollout at scale was presented.
critique: Personal anecdote with no data; the AI rollout process the speaker refers to is not described.
The employer in the story is unnamed, so the account cannot be checked.
